summary: For 11–12 year olds: energy conservation as bookkeeping — the TOTAL energy stays the same before and after a change, while individual stores redistribute. The central hurdle is the paradox that energy seems 'used up' (batteries go flat, pendulums die away) yet is said to be conserved. The resolution, taught explicitly, is that FUELS get used up while ENERGY is conserved but DISSIPATED — spread out, mostly to the thermal store of the surroundings, becoming too dispersed to reuse. The canonical confrontation is the pendulum or bouncing ball that doesn't return to its start height: this does not break conservation once the warmed surroundings are included in the account. Keep it qualitative-to-semi-quantitative; state the principle plainly ('energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between stores'), as the objective requires, but reserve efficiency and Sankey diagrams for the next tier. NOTE: as described, this topic straddles KS3→KS4 (England) and MS→HS (NGSS): conservation-as-total-unchanged is KS3/MS, but the named law and 'dissipation' are KS4/HS.
misconceptions: Believing energy is 'used up' or 'lost' — the central paradox; in fact fuels are used up while energy is conserved and dissipated.
Thinking the pendulum/ball that doesn't return to its start height disproves conservation — it ignores the energy dissipated to the surrounding air.
Treating 'wasted' energy as destroyed rather than spread out into low-grade thermal energy in the surroundings.
Confusing conserving energy (a physical law that always holds) with 'saving energy' (an everyday call to use less fuel).
Forgetting to include the surroundings in the system, so the energy account doesn't balance.
Assuming a perpetual-motion machine is possible — missing that dissipation always removes usable energy from the cycle.

activities.title: Energy budget with a locked total and a hidden-surroundings reveal
steps: Run a dissipative process you recognise (a bouncing ball that returns lower each time, a swinging pendulum that dies away, or a car braking to a stop) and watch the useful store (gravitational or kinetic) shrink.
With the surroundings hidden, notice that the energy appears to vanish — exactly the 'energy is lost' intuition.
Reveal the surroundings (e.g. a toggle) and watch the 'missing' joules reappear as a growing thermal store of the air, ground or brakes, so the total is accounted for.
Keep an eye on a TOTAL-energy bar held fixed throughout: it never changes height even as the store bars beneath it redistribute.

In a companion panel, drag a battery/fuel going flat and trace the energy transferred from its chemical store (by electrical and light/radiation pathways) until it ends up mostly in the thermal store of the surroundings — saying aloud 'the fuel is used up; the energy is conserved'.

Read the semi-quantitative joule values and watch the stores (including the surroundings) visibly reconcile to the fixed total — treat any actual numeric summing as optional, since contexts such as NGSS MS exclude energy calculations at this level while UK KS3 does permit quantifying energy.
activities.insight: 'Lost' energy has not been destroyed: it is dissipated — spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings — and once you include those surroundings the total energy is unchanged. Fuels are used up; energy conserves itself.

activities.title: Bend-a-paperclip prediction and feel test
steps: Take a metal paperclip and predict, with a reason, whether the bent spot will feel warmer, cooler, or the same if you bend it rapidly back and forth many times.
Bend it about twenty times at the same spot, then feel that spot (expect only a slight, just-detectable warming, not a dramatic rise).
Explain where the energy of your bending went, using the word 'dissipated' and naming the thermal store of the metal.

Consider the follow-ups: feel a ball and floor after many bounces for a tiny warming; explain why you can't collect that spread-out energy to make the ball bounce back up by itself; and reason why a machine cannot keep doing useful work forever — real machines always dissipate some energy to the surroundings and you can never get more energy out than you put in.
activities.insight: Repeatedly bending the metal does work on it that is transferred to its thermal store, warming the bent spot — the energy is not destroyed. This is a hands-on instance of dissipation, which connects to why a useful perpetual machine is impossible: real machines always spread some energy into the surroundings, where it cannot be fully recovered to do useful work, and no machine can give out more energy than is put in.

activities.title: Consolidation checks on conservation and dissipation
steps: Answer: the pendulum stops lower than it started — what happened to the energy? (Reject the 'it was destroyed' option and identify dissipation to the surroundings.)
Complete: energy is not lost but ___ (dissipated).

Redistribute the 'missing' joules to the thermal store of the surroundings so the total visibly matches the starting total — semi-quantitative, with the numeric step optional where energy calculations are excluded.
Decide true or false: 'energy is used up' — and justify the answer.
Explain what 'wasteful' means for a light bulb if energy is still conserved.
activities.insight: Dissipated energy is still part of the total once the surroundings are included in the account — it has moved to a less useful store (mostly the thermal store of the surroundings). 'Wasteful' means more energy transferred to unwanted stores, not energy destroyed; fuels, not energy, are consumed.

activities.title: Annotated before-and-after as a reference
steps: Study a before/after picture of a pendulum at its start swing versus settled at rest.

Reveal, on the settled state, that the missing energy very slightly warmed the surroundings (mainly the air, through air resistance, and the pivot, through friction); read the 'total energy: unchanged' callout.
Answer 'is energy lost?' and uncover the response 'no — dissipated to the surroundings'.
activities.insight: Names the idea and pre-empts 'lost' with 'dissipated', pairing a fixed-total statement with the warmed surroundings.

checkQuestion: A ball bounces a bit lower each time until it stops. People say the energy 'gets used up' and is lost. If energy can't be destroyed, where has the ball's energy actually gone — and why can't we get it all back to make it bounce forever?
checkAnswer: The energy isn't destroyed — each bounce transfers some of it, by heating and sound, to the surroundings (the floor, the air, and the ball warm very slightly). The total energy is unchanged; it has just spread out into the thermal store of the surroundings, too dispersed to gather back and lift the ball. So it's dissipated (spread out and less useful), not lost.
